derivations.claim: For every $t\geq1$, [A1] gives $P(U_t\leq\alpha)=\alpha$, so the test at that fixed time has level $\alpha$.
Independence in [A1] gives $P(U_t>\alpha\text{ for all }1\leq t\leq n)=\prod_{t=1}^nP(U_t>\alpha)=(1-\alpha)^n$. Taking the complement, $P(\exists t\leq n:U_t\leq\alpha)=1-(1-\alpha)^n$.

For $n\geq2$, $1-(1-\alpha)^n=\alpha+(1-\alpha)(1-(1-\alpha)^{n-1})>\alpha$, since both factors in the added term are positive. Thus the pointwise error bounds do not supply the same bound for all tests through time $n$.

A **discrete filtered probability space** is $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_0},P)$, where $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ is a probability space [[def-probability-measure]], each $\mathcal F_n$ is a sigma-algebra on $\Omega$ [[def-sigma-algebra]], and $\mathcal F_n\subseteq\mathcal F_{n+1}\subseteq\mathcal F$. The sequence $(\mathcal F_n)$ is a **filtration**. Time starts at zero. Neither completeness nor triviality of $\mathcal F_0$ is required.

Restriction of $P$ to $\mathcal F_n$ has total mass one and is countably additive: a disjoint sequence in $\mathcal F_n$ is also such a sequence in $\mathcal F$, with the same union and the same values of $P$. Thus each restriction is a probability measure. This specifies a structure and uses no choice principle. Real-valued processes will be the default.

On a filtered probability space [[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]], a **real stochastic process** is a sequence $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_0}$ of real random variables [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]] on the same space. It is **adapted** when $X_n^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal F_n$ for every $n$ and every real Borel set $B$. It is **integrable** when $E|X_n|<\infty$ for every $n$, using [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]].

An integrable adapted process satisfies both conditions at each fixed time. Integrability here does not mean $\sup_nE|X_n|<\infty$: the deterministic process $X_n=n$ has $E|X_n|=n<\infty$ at every time but unbounded supremum. Measurability and finiteness of each integral are separate requirements. No versions, limits or choices are selected.

On a discrete filtered probability space [[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]], a real process $(H_n)_{n\ge1}$ is **predictable** if $H_n$ is $\mathcal F_{n-1}$-measurable for every $n\ge1$. Real means finite-valued, as in [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. There is no $H_0$ convention and predictability alone imposes neither integrability nor boundedness.

Since $\mathcal F_{n-1}\subseteq\mathcal F_n$, every Borel preimage of $H_n$ is also in $\mathcal F_n$. Thus predictability implies adaptedness at the positive times. This is a preimage inclusion, requiring no choice or conditional expectation.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

Assume AC for the supplied existence theorem. Write $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ for the unique class in $L^1(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ consisting of conditional-expectation versions of $X$. A chosen real $\mathcal G$-measurable representative is a **version**. Equalities and inequalities involving these classes mean almost-sure equalities and inequalities.

Existence is [[thm-conditional-expectation-exists-by-radon-nikodym]] and uniqueness is [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]], applied to [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. The quotient is [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. If $X=X^{\ast}$ almost surely, [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]] gives identical event integrals, so the output class is independent of the input representative. The [[def-axiom-of-choice]] assumption is inherited from RN existence.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

Assume AC for existence. If $X\in L^1(P)$ and $Z$ is bounded real $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[ZX\mid\mathcal G]=ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. The identity also holds for finite real $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$ whenever $ZX$ and $ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ are integrable. In fact $X,ZX\in L^1$ imply the latter integrability.

Assume AC for existence. If $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ and $X\in L^1(P)$, then $E[E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ and $E[E[X\mid\mathcal H]\mid\mathcal G]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ almost surely. Also, if a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is $\mathcal H$-measurable, it is a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal H]$.

Assume AC [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. An integrable adapted real process $X$ [[def-adapted-and-integrable-stochastic-process]] is a **martingale**, **submartingale**, or **supermartingale** when, respectively, for every $n\ge0$,
$$E[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=X_n,\qquad E[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]\ge X_n,\qquad E[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]\le X_n\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
These are three separate conditions, with the convention that a submartingale has conditional future mean at least its present value. The conditional expectations are the almost-sure classes of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]; that supplier inherits AC from its Radon–Nikodym existence proof. The definition itself selects no representative and assumes no completed filtration.

The condition is imposed at each adjacent pair of times. An all-pairs formulation requires a proof. No boundedness or independence is part of this definition, and no trivial or deterministic initial value is imposed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC) [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\in\mathbb N_0})$ be a discrete filtration
on a measurable space, and let $\mathcal P_0$ be a family of probability laws
on $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$. A real-valued process $E=(E_t)_{t\in\mathbb N_0}$ is
a **nonnegative test supermartingale for $\mathcal P_0$** if, for every
$P\in\mathcal P_0$, it is adapted and integrable under $P$
[[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]]
[[def-martingale-submartingale-and-supermartingale]], satisfies
$P(E_t\ge0)=1$ for every $t$, and has $\mathbb E_P E_0\le1$.

The same process must satisfy the supermartingale condition under every law
in the null family; that is what makes the definition uniform over a composite
null. The initial value may be random and need not be bounded by one
pointwise. Time starts at zero.

Assume AC. Let $(\Lambda,\mathcal A,\pi)$ be a probability space and let
$\mathcal P_0$ be a family of laws on a common discrete filtered measurable
space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0})$. For each
$\lambda\in\Lambda$, let $E^\lambda=(E_t^\lambda)_{t\ge0}$ be a nonnegative
test supermartingale for $\mathcal P_0$. Suppose that, for every $t$, the map
$(\lambda,\omega)\mapsto E_t^\lambda(\omega)$ is measurable with respect to
$\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal F_t$. Before mixing, take its pointwise
nonnegative version $E_t^{\lambda,+}(\omega)=\max\{E_t^\lambda(\omega),0\}$,
and define
$$\overline E_t(\omega)=\int_\Lambda E_t^{\lambda,+}(\omega)\,\pi(d\lambda),\qquad \widetilde E_t(\omega)=\begin{cases}\overline E_t(\omega),&\overline E_t(\omega)<\infty,\\0,&\overline E_t(\omega)=\infty.\end{cases}$$
Then $\widetilde E=(\widetilde E_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a nonnegative test
supermartingale for $\mathcal P_0$. The modification on the infinite-integral
set makes a real-valued version common to all null laws.

Assume AC. Let $\mathcal P_0$ be a family of probability laws on a common
discrete filtered measurable space and let $E=(E_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a nonnegative
test supermartingale for $\mathcal P_0$
[[def-nonnegative-test-supermartingale]]. For every $P\in\mathcal P_0$ and
every $\alpha\in(0,1)$,
$$P\!\left(\sup_{t\ge0}E_t\ge\frac1\alpha\right)\le\alpha.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and fix a scale $c>0$. For $0\leq\lambda<1/c$, define
$$\psi_{E,c}(\lambda):=\frac{-\log(1-c\lambda)-c\lambda}{c^2}.$$
On a discrete filtered probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\in\mathbb N_0},P)$, a pair of real processes $(S_t,V_t)_{t\in\mathbb N_0}$ is a **one-sided sub-exponential pair at scale $c$** when $S_0=V_0=0$, $V_t\geq0$, and both processes are $\mathcal F_t$-measurable at each time, and for every $\lambda\in[0,1/c)$ there is a real process $(L_t^\lambda)_{t\in\mathbb N_0}$ that is nonnegative, integrable, and $\mathcal F_t$-measurable at each time, satisfies $\mathbb E L_0^\lambda\leq1$ and $\mathbb E[L_t^\lambda\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]\leq L_{t-1}^\lambda$ almost surely for each $t\geq1$, and obeys
$$\exp\!\left(\lambda S_t-\psi_{E,c}(\lambda)V_t\right)\leq L_t^\lambda\quad\text{almost surely for every }t\geq0.$$

For $\alpha\in(0,1)$, a Borel-measurable function $u:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ is a **one-sided sub-exponential uniform boundary with crossing probability $\alpha$ and scale $c$** if, for every discrete filtered probability space and every one-sided sub-exponential pair at scale $c$,
$$P\!\left(\exists t\geq1:S_t\geq u(V_t)\right)\leq\alpha.$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

$$\exp(x)\to+\infty\quad(x\to+\infty),\qquad \exp(x)\to0\quad(x\to-\infty),$$
and the range of $\exp$ is contained in $(0,\infty)$ and is unbounded above with infimum $0$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Every function differentiable at $c$ is continuous at $c$.
If $f,g$ are real functions differentiable at $c$, then $f+g$ and $fg$ are
differentiable there and
$$
(f+g)'(c)=f'(c)+g'(c),\qquad (fg)'(c)=f'(c)g(c)+f(c)g'(c).
$$
If $g(c)\ne0$, then $f/g$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$$
(f/g)'(c)=\frac{f'(c)g(c)-f(c)g'(c)}{g(c)^2}.
$$
If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, $g$ is differentiable at $f(c)$, and the
composition is defined near $c$, then $g\circ f$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$(g\circ f)'(c)=g'(f(c))f'(c)$. For every integer $m\ge1$,
$(x^m)'=mx^{m-1}$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g(A) \subseteq B$, and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$. If $g$ is continuous
at $c$ and $f$ is continuous at $g(c) \in B$, then $f \circ g$ is continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $g$ is continuous on $A$ and $f$ is continuous on $B$, then
$f \circ g$ is continuous on $A$.

**No side hypothesis is needed, and that is the whole point.** The composition
theorem for limits, [[thm-composition-of-function-limits]], must assume one of
two extra conditions: either $L \in B$ with $f(L) = M$, or $g \ne L$ on a
punctured neighbourhood of $c$; with both dropped the statement is false, which
is [[fs-naive-composition-of-limits]]. The first of those conditions is exactly
*continuity of $f$ at $L$* written out, so under the hypotheses above it holds
automatically and nothing has to be assumed. The mechanism is visible in the
proof: [[def-continuity-real]] quantifies over $|y - b| < \rho$ rather than over
$0 < |y - b| < \rho$, so the value $y = b$ that the limit version cannot control
is precisely the one the continuity hypothesis does control.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\in\mathbb N_0},P)$ be a discrete filtered probability space and let $(\theta_t)_{t\geq1}$ be a real target process with each $\theta_t$ measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_t$. For $\alpha\in(0,1)$, a sequence of random closed intervals $C_t=[L_t,U_t]$, with finite real $\mathcal F_t$-measurable endpoints at each $t\geq1$, is a **$(1-\alpha)$ confidence sequence for the target process $(\theta_t)$** if
$$P\!\left(\theta_t\in C_t\text{ for every }t\geq1\right)\geq1-\alpha.$$
The target may be random and may vary with time; the definition asserts only simultaneous coverage under the specified probability law.

Inputs are real bounds $a\leq b$, a nominal error level $\delta\in(0,1)$, an observation stream $(X_t)_{t\geq1}$ with $X_t\in[a,b]$ almost surely and $X_t$ measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_t$, a forecast stream $(\widehat X_t)_{t\geq1}$ with $\widehat X_t\in[a,b]$ almost surely and $\widehat X_t$ measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_{t-1}$, and, when $c=b-a>0$, an evaluation procedure for a Borel one-sided sub-exponential uniform boundary $u_{\delta/2,c}$ with crossing probability $\delta/2$ and scale $c$. The output is one interval $C_t$ at each positive integer time $t$.

1. If $c=0$, return $C_t=[a,a]$ at each time.

2. If $c>0$, initialize $\bar X_0=0$ and $V_0=0$. After receiving forecast $\widehat X_t$ and then observation $X_t$, update
$$\bar X_t=\left(1-\frac1t\right)\bar X_{t-1}+\frac{X_t}{t},\qquad V_t=V_{t-1}+(X_t-\widehat X_t)^2.$$
Return
$$C_t=\left[\bar X_t-\frac{u_{\delta/2,c}(V_t)}{t},\;\bar X_t+\frac{u_{\delta/2,c}(V_t)}{t}\right].$$

The procedure uses observations only through time $t$. The accumulated quantity $V_t$ is the observed sum of squared forecast errors; it is not a predictable conditional-variance process.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: If $c=0$, then $X_t=\widehat X_t=a$ almost surely for every $t$. By [F6], each $m_t=a$ almost surely, so $\mu_t=a$ simultaneously almost surely and the algorithm's singleton $C_t=[a,a]$ covers it. If $c>0$, boundedness gives $X_t\in L^1(P)$; choose the versions in the Statement using [A1]. Any two versions agree almost surely by [F5], and the countable union of their exceptional null sets is null, so the all-times coverage probability does not depend on those choices.

For $x>-1$ define $r(x)=(x-\log(1+x))/x^2$ when $x\ne0$ and $r(0)=1/2$. Direct integration gives $r(x)=\int_0^1 t/(1+tx)\,dt$. The integrand decreases in $x$ for every $t>0$, so $r$ is decreasing on $(-1,\infty)$. If $c>0$, $0<\lambda<1/c$, and $|\xi|\leq c$, then $x=\lambda\xi\geq-\lambda c>-1$, whence $\lambda\xi-\log(1+\lambda\xi)=(\lambda\xi)^2r(\lambda\xi)\leq(\lambda\xi)^2r(-\lambda c)=\psi_{E,c}(\lambda)\xi^2$. Exponentiating yields $\exp(\lambda\xi-\psi_{E,c}(\lambda)\xi^2)\leq1+\lambda\xi$; the same holds at $\lambda=0$ by equality.

Fix any one-sided sub-exponential pair at scale $c>0$ and any finite mixture parameters from the Statement. For each $j$, its defining condition [F13] supplies a dominating nonnegative test supermartingale $L^{\lambda_j}$. For $x=c\lambda_j\in(0,1)$, define $h(t)=-\log(1-t)-t$ on $t<1$. By [F17], $h(0)=0$ and the chain and sum rules give $h'(t)=1/(1-t)-1=t/(1-t)$. The function is continuous on $[0,x]$ and differentiable on $(0,x)$ by [F17]. As $s\to-\infty$, each affine exponent tends to $-\infty$, so [F14] makes every term tend to zero; the finite sum tends to zero. Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.
If $Y,Z$ are conditional-expectation versions of the same real integrable $X$ given $\mathcal G$, then $Y=Z$ almost surely.

Inputs are real bounds $a\leq b$, a nominal error level $\delta\in(0,1)$, an observation stream $(X_t)_{t\geq1}$ with $X_t\in[a,b]$ almost surely and $X_t$ measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_t$, a forecast stream $(\widehat X_t)_{t\geq1}$ with $\widehat X_t\in[a,b]$ almost surely and $\widehat X_t$ measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_{t-1}$, and, when $c=b-a>0$, an evaluation procedure for a Borel one-sided sub-exponential uniform boundary $u_{\delta/2,c}$ with crossing probability $\delta/2$ and scale $c$. The output is one interval $C_t$ at each positive integer time $t$.

1. If $c=0$, return $C_t=[a,a]$ at each time.

2. If $c>0$, initialize $\bar X_0=0$ and $V_0=0$. After receiving forecast $\widehat X_t$ and then observation $X_t$, update
$$\bar X_t=\left(1-\frac1t\right)\bar X_{t-1}+\frac{X_t}{t},\qquad V_t=V_{t-1}+(X_t-\widehat X_t)^2.$$
Return
$$C_t=\left[\bar X_t-\frac{u_{\delta/2,c}(V_t)}{t},\;\bar X_t+\frac{u_{\delta/2,c}(V_t)}{t}\right].$$

The procedure uses observations only through time $t$. The accumulated quantity $V_t$ is the observed sum of squared forecast errors; it is not a predictable conditional-variance process.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\in\mathbb N_0},P)$ be a discrete filtered probability space, let $a\leq b$ be real numbers, and put $c=b-a$. Let $(X_t)_{t\geq1}$ be real with $X_t$ measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_t$ and $P(a\leq X_t\leq b)=1$ for every $t$. Let $(\widehat X_t)_{t\geq1}$ be real with $\widehat X_t$ measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_{t-1}$ and $P(a\leq\widehat X_t\leq b)=1$ for every $t$. Fix $\delta\in(0,1)$ and write $\alpha=\delta/2$. For $c>0$, let $u_{\alpha,c}$ be any Borel one-sided sub-exponential uniform boundary with crossing probability $\alpha$ at scale $c$. Choose any versions $m_t=E[X_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]$ and define
$$\bar X_t=\frac1t\sum_{i=1}^tX_i,\qquad \mu_t=\frac1t\sum_{i=1}^tm_i,\qquad V_t=\sum_{i=1}^t(X_i-\widehat X_i)^2.$$
Let $C_t$ be the interval returned at time $t$ by the empirical-Bernstein interval-update algorithm, using $u_{\alpha,c}$ when $c>0$. Then
$$P\!\left(\mu_t\in C_t\text{ for every }t\geq1\right)\geq1-\delta.$$
The probability statement is independent of the chosen conditional-expectation versions. No common conditional mean is assumed. If there is a fixed real $\mu$ such that $E[X_i\mid\mathcal F_{i-1}]=\mu$ almost surely for every $i$, then $\mu_t=\mu$ simultaneously almost surely and the same intervals cover this fixed mean.

For $c>0$, the finite-mixture formula also supplies a valid boundary: choose an integer $J\geq1$, numbers $0<\lambda_j<1/c$, and weights $w_j>0$ with $\sum_{j=1}^Jw_j=1$. For every $v\geq0$, the unique nonnegative solution $s=u_{\alpha,c}(v)$ of
$$\sum_{j=1}^Jw_j\exp\!\left(\lambda_js-\psi_{E,c}(\lambda_j)v\right)=\frac1\alpha$$
defines a Borel one-sided sub-exponential uniform boundary with crossing probability $\alpha$ at scale $c$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.
